title: Numerical Solutions of PDEs: Elliptic, Parabolic, and Hyperbolic Fields
text:
A general linear second-order partial differential equation in two dimensions has the form: \[A \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + B \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} + C \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + D \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + E \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + F u = G\]
The physical nature of the problem and its numerical behavior depend on the discriminant \(\Delta = B^2 - 4AC\):

section: 2. Elliptic PDEs: The Poisson Equation on a Discrete Grid
text:
2. Elliptic PDEs: The Poisson Equation on a Discrete Grid
Consider the 2D Poisson equation on a square domain: \[\nabla^2 \phi = \frac{\partial^2 \phi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \phi}{\partial y^2} = -\frac{\rho(x, y)}{\varepsilon_0}\]
We discretize the domain with grid spacing \(\Delta x = \Delta y = h\): \[x_i = i h, \qquad y_j = j h, \qquad \phi_{i,j} \approx \phi(x_i, y_j)\]
Using second-order central difference approximations: \[\left. \frac{\partial^2 \phi}{\partial x^2} \right|_{i,j} \approx \frac{\phi_{i+1,j} - 2\phi_{i,j} + \phi_{i-1,j}}{h^2}\] \[\left. \frac{\partial^2 \phi}{\partial y^2} \right|_{i,j} \approx \frac{\phi_{i,j+1} - 2\phi_{i,j} + \phi_{i,j-1}}{h^2}\]
Adding both terms yields the 5-point discrete Laplacian stencil: \[\frac{\phi_{i+1,j} + \phi_{i-1,j} + \phi_{i,j+1} + \phi_{i,j-1} - 4\phi_{i,j}}{h^2} = -\frac{\rho_{i,j}}{\varepsilon_0}\]
Solving for the central value \(\phi_{i,j}\): \[\boxed{\phi_{i,j} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \phi_{i+1,j} + \phi_{i-1,j} + \phi_{i,j+1} + \phi_{i,j-1} \right) + \frac{h^2}{4\varepsilon_0} \rho_{i,j}}\]

Iterative Relaxation Schemes

Jacobi Iteration: Computes the \((k+1)\)-th grid state strictly using values from the \(k\)-th iteration: \[\phi_{i,j}^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \phi_{i+1,j}^{(k)} + \phi_{i-1,j}^{(k)} + \phi_{i,j+1}^{(k)} + \phi_{i,j-1}^{(k)} \right) + \frac{h^2}{4\varepsilon_0} \rho_{i,j}\]
Gauss-Seidel Iteration: Immediately uses updated values as soon as they are computed: \[\phi_{i,j}^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \phi_{i+1,j}^{(k)} + \phi_{i-1,j}^{(k+1)} + \phi_{i,j+1}^{(k)} + \phi_{i,j-1}^{(k+1)} \right) + \frac{h^2}{4\varepsilon_0} \rho_{i,j}\] Converges twice as fast as Jacobi.
Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR): Accelerates convergence by extrapolating with parameter \(\omega \in (1, 2)\): \[\phi_{i,j}^{(k+1)} = (1 - \omega) \phi_{i,j}^{(k)} + \omega \phi_{i,j}^{\text{GS}}\] Optimal parameter for an \(N \times N\) grid: \(\omega_{\text{opt}} \approx \frac{2}{1 + \pi / N}\).

title: Syllabus & Course Rules
text:
The only crucial prerequisite is programming using basic Python at the level of PHYB57. If you are rusty in Python, refresh your practical skills ASAP.
This course assumes you are interested in: 1. Intermediate and advanced numerical methods used in physical sciences. 2. HPC (High Performance Computing), including parallelization of algorithms. 3. Coding in one of the HPC languages more powerful than Python.
After this course, you will understand programs in both C(++) and modern Fortran. You will be required to actively express your ideas in one of those languages. You must acquire passive knowledge of C(++) AND Fortran, and active knowledge of C(++) OR Fortran.

title: Syllabus & Course Rules
text:
📜 Detailed Contents of the Course

1. Structure and scope of the course. Numerical Computing in Physical Sciences: History and Contemporary efforts.
2. HPC: need for speed, why and how. History and modernity: microprocessors, Unix, Linux, and Internet. Intro to Linux (CentOS).
3. Connectivity (ssh & sftp, traceroute & ping). Basic Linux shells and commands. Recommended compilers (GNU, Intel, Nvidia). Simple C/F95 vs Python benchmarks.
4. C and Fortran 95 - compilers, basic usage. Numerical puzzle of 711. Kruskal counts and linked lists. Integration with Python.
5. More Fortran. Monte Carlo method. Parallel execution on CPU using OpenMP fork-join method in loops.
6. Modern computing in the era of Integrated Circuits. Appearence of barriers to single-thread computing. Moore’s law.
7. CPU and MIC (Xeon Phi). Supercomputers and supercomputing. More C. Multi-dimensional arrays in C vs. Fortran.
8. Parallelization via OpenMP in C and F. Segmentation faults. Bottlenecks (Computation vs RAM bandwidth). Graphics in Fortran/C (DISLIN).
9. Computations with CPU vs. MIC vs. CUDA. Automatic vectorization. N-body integration methods. Basic Neural Net: teaching a broom to stand upside down.
10. Interaction of protoplanets with 3D particle and gas disks. Eulerian vs. Lagrangian methods. Fourier integral & discrete transform (FFT). Aliasing. Simple GPU programs in CUDA Fortran.
11. Simple GPU programs in CUDA C/C++. Introduction to MPI. What are NNs and why do they work. Machine Learning. Optimum Search: Simplex (Nelder-Mead) method.
12. Presentation of your A4 group projects.

title: High-Performance PDE Solvers: C++, Fortran 90 & Interactive Heat Diffusion
text:
3. Fortran 90: High-Performance 2D Advection Solver
! advection_2d.f90
! Compile: gfortran -O3 -std=f2018 advection_2d.f90 -o advection_sim
program advection_solver
    implicit none
    integer, parameter :: N = 256
    real(8) :: u(0:N, 0:N), u_new(0:N, 0:N)
    real(8) :: c_x, c_y, dx, dy, dt
    integer :: i, j, step, n_steps

    dx = 1.0d0 / dble(N)
    dy = 1.0d0 / dble(N)
    c_x = 1.0d0; c_y = 1.0d0
    dt = 0.4d0 * dx / sqrt(c_x**2 + c_y**2) ! CFL stability criterion

    ! Initialize 2D Gaussian pulse
    do j = 0, N
        do i = 0, N
            u(i, j) = exp(-((i*dx - 0.3d0)**2 + (j*dy - 0.3d0)**2) / 0.02d0)
        end do
    end do

    n_steps = 500
    ! Lax-Wendroff 2D advection scheme
    do step = 1, n_steps
        do j = 1, N - 1
            do i = 1, N - 1
                u_new(i, j) = u(i, j) - 0.5d0 * (c_x * dt / dx) * (u(i+1, j) - u(i-1, j)) &
                                      - 0.5d0 * (c_y * dt / dy) * (u(i, j+1) - u(i, j-1))
            end do
        end do
        u = u_new
    end do

    print *, "2D Advection successfully integrated for ", n_steps, " time steps."
end program advection_solver
